title: China’s Development Finance and Critical Mineral Acquisitions: Evidence of a Strategic Quid Pro Quo
text:
Across Africa, China’s role as a major development financier has expanded in tandem with its growing presence in the critical minerals sector. Policymakers often treat these two domains as separate tracks, governed by different actors, institutions, and motivations. Yet countries that receive larger volumes of Chinese development finance are also far more likely to see Chinese companies acquire significant mining assets in the years that follow. This pattern does not imply explicit conditionality or contractual linkage. Instead, it reveals a broader strategic logic: infrastructure, diplomatic engagement, and resource access are mutually reinforcing within China’s approach to Africa, and African governments often engage with China in similarly bundled ways.
Africa’s mineral endowments such as cobalt in the Democratic Republic of Congo, copper in Zambia, manganese in Gabon, graphite in Mozambique sit at the heart of the clean energy transition. These minerals determine the trajectory of global supply chains for electric vehicles, batteries, and renewable power systems. At the same time, China has become Africa’s single largest bilateral financier, funding roads, power plants, railways, transmission lines, and industrial parks through a combination of policy bank loans, state-owned enterprises, and commercial partners. While Western institutions tend to compartmentalize sectors, China frequently engages countries through vertically integrated political-economic relationships that combine infrastructure, trade, industrial policy, and diplomatic cooperation.

title: China’s Development Finance and Critical Mineral Acquisitions: Evidence of a Strategic Quid Pro Quo
text:
What I did
This research brings together two large datasets–a comprehensive record of Chinese development finance from AidData and detailed mining transaction data from SNL Metals & Mining from S&P Global–to analyze how these relationships unfold over time. The approach is straightforward: track the years in which African countries receive significant Chinese development finance and examine whether Chinese firms acquire mines in those same countries. Across over fifty countries and two decades, the results are clear. The significant rises of Chinese development finance following years of Chinese mining acquisitions. The relationship strengthens over time and is especially pronounced in minerals central to China’s industrial and energy transition priorities, including cobalt, copper, nickel, and uranium.
Importantly, the data provide no support for claims that China uses explicit “infrastructure-for-resources” conditions. No contractual quid pro quo is evident. Instead, the pattern reflects a relational form of state capitalism. Development finance builds political goodwill, deepens elite networks, and lowers transaction costs for Chinese firms seeking to enter or expand in resource sectors. Infrastructure projects also address long-standing bottlenecks such as electricity shortages or transport constraints that improve the commercial viability of mining investment. African governments, in turn, often view partnerships with China holistically. A country negotiating a major railway loan or hydropower project may also be seeking buyers for brownfield mineral assets or investors for new extraction ventures. In this context, development finance and mineral investment become mutually legible components of a broader diplomatic and economic relationship.
This stands in contrast to Western engagement. Development projects financed by the World Bank, African Development Bank, USAID, or the EU show no comparable relationship with Western mining acquisitions. Western development institutions operate through highly segmented systems, where infrastructure lending, diplomatic outreach, and private-sector investment rarely move in coordinated ways. China’s model is not necessarily superior, but it is more integrated, allowing its firms to move quickly when opportunities arise.

title: China’s Development Finance and Critical Mineral Acquisitions: Evidence of a Strategic Quid Pro Quo
text:
Implications
The implications are significant. For African governments, understanding this dynamic is critical for negotiating better terms. Bundled engagement can offer real advantages such as faster project delivery, flexible financing, and complementary investments, but it can also generate risks, including reduced bargaining power or overreliance on a single partner. Strategic competition between China and Western countries can, if managed well, help African states secure higher standards, more diversified financing, and greater local value addition in mineral processing and manufacturing.
For Western governments and multilateral institutions, the findings point to a structural competitive gap. The global energy transition requires resilient supply chains for critical minerals, yet Western development finance remains siloed from industrial and strategic objectives. Efforts to counterbalance China’s influence will require more than rhetoric about de-risking or fair minerals sourcing. They will require integrated approaches that combine infrastructure financing, commercial support, policy coordination, and long-term partnerships with African governments.
For China, the results reveal the importance of transparency and governance. While relational engagement has advantages, it also generates misunderstanding and suspicion abroad. Strengthening environmental standards, ensuring contract transparency, and supporting African industrialization would help China demonstrate that its approach can create broadly shared development benefits, not only secure mineral access.
The global energy transition has intensified the interdependence between infrastructure, diplomacy, and natural resources. China already operates with an understanding of this nexus. The evidence presented here suggests that development finance can meaningfully shape the geography of mineral investments, not through coercive deals, but through the cumulative political and economic relationships it builds. As demand for critical minerals accelerates, the future of development finance is increasingly intertwined with the future of industrial strategy and global climate politics. Policymakers who continue treating these domains as separate will find themselves at a disadvantage.

title: Research

Working papers

Is There a Development Quid Pro Quo? Chinese Finance and Critical Mineral Access in Africa
Revise and resubmit
The impact of China’s engagement in Africa has drawn much attention in scholarly debates. Some critics view China’s interest in Africa as a form of neocolonialism, arguing that China is extracting natural resources for its own state interests. China has been involved in numerous mining activities across the continent, gaining access to critical minerals such as cobalt and copper, which are strategically important for national energy security. At the same time, China has also financed many development projects to help African countries address pressing development challenges. Using multiple datasets on development finance and mining properties, this paper examines whether Chinese development finance coincides with its mine acquisitions in 53 African countries, and if so, which minerals are associated with which type of Chinese finance. The results show that minerals needed for clean energy technologies such as copper, cobalt, nickel, and platinum group metals are significantly associated with Chinese loan commitments to recipient countries, while uranium is the mineral most strongly linked to development projects, particularly those including a substantial grant component and highly concessional repayment terms. This paper carries significant policy implications for global energy transitions, critical mineral supply chains, and development finance by revealing how various financial instruments are associated with critical minerals and by highlighting the need for more transparent development practices.

Why Energy Infrastructure Investment Delivers Delayed Electricity Access
with J. Guan and P. Jagger · Under review
Nearly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa lack access to electricity, even as foreign-financed generation and transmission capacity has expanded rapidly. Whether that investment reaches households, and how quickly, is rarely measured, because energy projects are typically evaluated by whether they were built and how much capacity they added, not by whether nearby communities gained access. Zambia, a major recipient of Chinese energy finance and the first African country to default on its external debt during the COVID-19 pandemic, offers a rare test. We link a staggered portfolio of Chinese-financed power plants and transmission lines completed between 2014 and 2019 to the national utility’s geocoded grid maps and to satellite-derived, settlement-level electricity access data, forming a pixel-level panel for 2013–2020. We find that, in rural areas where baseline access is lowest, access gains appear only around six years after completion, while urban centers, where the access index is already at its ceiling, show no measurable change. Estimates by asset type suggest that areas near new transmission lines respond earlier than areas served by new generation. These divergent timelines are consistent with a coordination failure in which new generation capacity remains unused until distribution networks and household connections catch up, whereas transmission projects link communities to generation that already exists. Our findings suggest that financing for new generation should be paired with investment in distribution networks and connection programs, with explicit access targets written into financing agreements, if new capacity is to reach communities quickly.


Industrial Electrification in the Global South: China’s Potential Role
with C. Springer
Industrial electrification is central to decarbonizing industry in the Global South, where industrial output and emissions are expected to grow rapidly. China, the world’s largest manufacturer of clean energy technologies and a major source of development finance, is well positioned to support this transition, yet its potential role remains poorly understood. This paper assesses that role through industrial heat pumps, a near-commercial technology that can replace fossil fuel boilers for low- and medium-temperature process heat. We first map China’s industrial heat pump manufacturing through a structured review of English- and Chinese-language sources, corroborated by expert interviews, and analyze Chinese heat pump exports using UN Comtrade data for 2018-2023. We then develop a push-pull framework, using principal component analysis to combine indicators of Chinese trade, development finance, and power-sector presence (push) with indicators of each country’s readiness to adopt industrial heat pumps (pull). We find that China’s industrial heat pump sector is held back by limited demand and deployment experience, not technical capacity alone, and that its heat pump exports flow mainly to high-income OECD markets. Push exposure is concentrated in Southeast Asia and parts of Africa, while pull potential closely tracks each country’s stage of industrial and energy development. Vietnam and Brazil emerge as the most promising partners, combining deep Chinese engagement with favorable domestic conditions. These results suggest that China can act as a scaled provider of equipment and finance in more industrialized markets, while in less developed ones its contribution lies in building the grid and industrial foundations that electrification requires.

title: Congyi Dai
text:
Welcome!
I study how China’s dominance in clean energy manufacturing, critical mineral processing, and overseas infrastructure finance is reshaping the global energy transition, with a focus on Africa and the wider Global South. My work draws on economics, political science, and environmental studies, and combines causal inference with geospatial analysis of large geocoded datasets.
I am a Postdoctoral Associate in the Science, Technology and International Affairs (STIA) program at Georgetown University’s Walsh School of Foreign Service, where I work with Joanna Lewis on US-China competition in clean energy supply chains. I received my Ph.D. from the University of Michigan School for Environment & Sustainability in 2026. My dissertation, China’s Role in Shaping Energy Access in Africa, examines how Chinese development finance shapes both access to critical minerals and access to electricity across the continent. Before Georgetown, I was a Global China Pre-doctoral Fellow at Boston University Global Development Policy Center. I have also worked in the World Bank in Washington D.C and United Nations Development Programme in Port Louis, Mauritius.
